Apple___Apple_scab.overview: Apple scab is caused by the fungus Venturia inaequalis. It produces olive-green to black velvety spots on leaves and fruit, causing leaf distortion and scabby lesions on apples.
symptoms: Olive-green to dark brown velvety circular lesions on young leaves
Leaves turn yellow and drop prematurely, causing early defoliation
Corky, scabby brown lesions on fruits that may crack as they grow
non_chemical_management: Rake and destroy fallen leaves in autumn to reduce overwintering ascospore inoculum
Prune tree canopy annually in dormant season to improve air circulation and rapid leaf drying
Apply urea spray (5%) to fallen leaves in autumn to accelerate decomposition
prevention: Plant scab-resistant apple cultivars (e.g., Prima, Priscilla, Enterprise) where suitable
Maintain wide tree spacing and avoid low-lying frost pockets with prolonged morning dew
treatment: Protective foliar spray of Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L at green tip and pink bud stages
At petal fall, apply Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 ml/L or Captan 50% WP @ 2.5 g/L
Dodine 65% WP @ 1.0 g/L can be used early season for high-pressure curative action
safety_precautions: Follow Pre-Harvest Interval (PHI) of 21 days for Difenoconazole
Wear protective chemical apron, face shield, and chemical-resistant gloves
Do not spray during full bloom to protect pollinating honeybees
source_references: ICAR-CITH (Central Institute of Temperate Horticulture) - Apple Disease Guide (https://cith.icar.gov.in)
TNAU Agritech Portal (Crop Protection - Apple Scab) (https://agritech.tnau.ac.in)

Apple___Black_rot.overview: Black rot is caused by the fungus Botryosphaeria obtusa. It affects leaves (frogeye leaf spot), branches (cankers), and ripening fruits with firm, dark rotting rings.
symptoms: Small purple specks on leaves expanding into circular 'frogeye' spots with tan centers
Sunken, reddish-brown bark cankers on limbs and trunks
Firm, concentric dark brown to black rot on fruits leading to dried mummified apples
non_chemical_management: Prune out dead wood, fire blight strikes, and cankered limbs at least 15 cm below infected tissue
Remove and bury all dried mummified fruit remaining on the tree or orchard floor
Disinfect pruning shears in 70% alcohol or 10% sodium hypochlorite between cuts
prevention: Maintain tree vigor through balanced fertilization and adequate watering
Avoid mechanical damage to bark and trunks during mowing and harvesting
treatment: Apply Captan 50% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L starting at silver tip through second cover
Thiophanate-methyl 70% WP @ 1.0 g/L can be combined for broad canker suppression
safety_precautions: Maintain a 14-day Pre-Harvest Interval for Captan
Ensure full PPE coverage and avoid skin contact
source_references: ICAR-CITH Temperate Orchard Management Bulletins
University Extension Apple Pathology Compendium

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.overview: Cedar apple rust is caused by the heteroecious fungus Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae. It requires both apple and Eastern red cedar (Juniperus) to complete its lifecycle.
symptoms: Bright orange-yellow circular spots on the upper leaf surface in spring
Small orange droplets form on upper leaf spots, followed by cylindrical tube-like structures on undersides
Severe infections cause defoliation and fruit dwarfing
non_chemical_management: Remove and destroy galls from nearby juniper and cedar trees in late winter before spring rains
Where feasible, remove Eastern red cedar trees within a 300 to 500 meter radius of the orchard
Collect and dispose of heavily blighted leaves
prevention: Plant resistant apple varieties (e.g., Liberty, Freedom, Enterprise)
Avoid planting junipers as ornamental windbreaks near apple orchards
treatment: Apply Myclobutanil 10% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L from pink bud until 2 weeks after petal fall
Triazole fungicides like Tebuconazole 25.9% EC @ 0.75 ml/L provide strong curative control
safety_precautions: Adhere to a 14-day harvest interval for Myclobutanil
Do not spray directly over waterways to protect aquatic organisms
source_references: ICAR Apple Crop Protection Bulletin
Penn State Extension Tree Fruit Production Guide

Apple___healthy.overview: The apple foliage is vibrant, healthy, and free of visible fungal lesions, scabs, or insect damage.
symptoms: Uniform green leaf color with no chlorosis or necrosis
Smooth leaf surface without spots, galls, or powdery growth
non_chemical_management: Maintain open-center or central-leader pruning for good canopy ventilation
Apply balanced NPK fertilizer based on annual soil testing
Keep orchard floor mulched or mowed to reduce weed competition
prevention: Regular weekly scouting across orchard rows for early detection of scab or aphids
Ensure adequate winter chilling hours and irrigation during fruit sizing
safety_precautions: No chemical interventions are necessary or recommended for healthy apple trees.
source_references: ICAR-CITH Good Agricultural Practices for Apple Orchards

Blueberry___healthy.overview: The blueberry plant displays healthy green foliage without signs of mummy berry, rust, or iron chlorosis.
symptoms: Deep green, glossy leaves with clear venation
Vigorous new cane growth and healthy flower/fruit clusters
non_chemical_management: Maintain acidic soil pH between 4.5 and 5.2 using elemental sulfur as needed
Apply a 7-10 cm layer of pine bark or sawdust mulch to retain soil moisture and suppress weeds
Prune older canes (over 5 years) annually in late winter to promote productive new shoots
prevention: Use drip irrigation to keep bush canopies dry and reduce fungal risk
Ensure well-drained raised beds to prevent Phytophthora root rot
safety_precautions: No chemical pesticides are required for healthy blueberry bushes.
source_references: University Horticultural Extension - Blueberry Health & Management

Cherry___healthy.overview: The cherry tree foliage is healthy and free from powdery mildew, leaf spot, and bacterial canker.
symptoms: Smooth, lustrous green leaves without curling, shot-holes, or powdery residues
Healthy fruit development without brown rot or cracking
non_chemical_management: Prune branches during dry summer weather to avoid bacterial canker entry points
Ensure uniform soil moisture through drip irrigation to prevent fruit cracking
Mow ground cover to minimize humidity buildup under tree canopies
prevention: Scout weekly for black cherry aphids and powdery mildew in early spring
Paint lower trunks with white latex paint to avoid winter sunscald
safety_precautions: No chemical fungicides or insecticides are needed for healthy cherry foliage.
source_references: ICAR-CITH Temperate Fruit Production Guidelines

Cherry___Powdery_mildew.overview: Powdery mildew on cherry is caused by the fungus Podosphaera clandestina. It infects young leaves, terminal shoots, and developing cherries, coating them in white talcum-like mycelium.
symptoms: White powdery patches on the undersides of leaves and on young terminal shoots
Infected leaves curl upward, become brittle, and drop prematurely
White fungal growth and webbed blemishes on developing cherry fruits
non_chemical_management: Prune crowded water sprouts and terminal shoots to open canopy to direct sunlight
Avoid excessive late-season nitrogen fertilizers that stimulate susceptible tender flushes
Irrigate early in the day to allow foliage to dry before nightfall
prevention: Plant orchards with adequate row spacing and oriented parallel to prevailing winds
Monitor tender new flushes closely during warm, humid spring weather
treatment: Apply Wettable Sulphur 80% WDG @ 2.5 g/L at petal fall and shuck-fall stages
For active infections, spray Myclobutanil 10% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Hexaconazole 5% EC @ 1.0 ml/L
Potassium bicarbonate @ 3.0 g/L can be used as an organic foliar spray
safety_precautions: Do not apply sulfur when temperatures exceed 30°C to prevent phytotoxic leaf burn
Observe a 14-day Pre-Harvest Interval for synthetic systemic fungicides
source_references: ICAR-CITH Temperate Stone Fruit Protection Manual
Washington State University Extension Tree Fruit Pathology

Corn___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray_leaf_sp.overview: Gray leaf spot is caused by Cercospora zeae-maydis. It creates narrow, rectangular tan to gray lesions bounded by leaf veins, severely impairing photosynthesis and stalk integrity.
symptoms: Small, tan spots surrounded by yellow halos, expanding into long rectangular lesions
Lesions strictly restricted by parallel leaf veins (1-6 cm long)
Coalescing lesions cause entire leaves to wither and blight, leading to stalk rot and lodging
non_chemical_management: Incorporate crop residues deeply with moldboard plowing to accelerate fungal decomposition
Rotate maize with non-host crops (soybean, groundnut, cotton) for at least 1-2 years
Avoid overly high plant populations that restrict airflow through the canopy
prevention: Select maize hybrids with high genetic tolerance or resistance to Cercospora
Plant early in the season to avoid peak disease pressure during grain filling
treatment: Apply Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Difenoconazole 11.4% SC @ 1.0 ml/L at tasseling (VT/R1)
Alternatively, foliar spray of Pyraclostrobin 20% WG @ 1.0 g/L or Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L
safety_precautions: Follow Pre-Harvest Interval of 30 days before harvest for grain or silage
Avoid spraying near water bodies; toxic to fish
source_references: ICAR-IIMR (Indian Institute of Maize Research) Disease Bulletin (https://iimr.icar.gov.in)
Purdue University Extension - Gray Leaf Spot in Field Corn

Corn___Common_rust.overview: Common rust is caused by Puccinia sorghi. It is characterized by powdery, golden to reddish-brown pustules erupting on both upper and lower leaf surfaces during cool, humid conditions.
symptoms: Small, circular to elongate reddish-brown pustules on both leaf surfaces
Pustules rupture the epidermis to release powdery cinnamon-brown urediniospores
Chlorosis and necrosis around pustules in heavy infections
non_chemical_management: Plant resistant hybrids containing Rp single-gene or multi-gene resistance
Scout lower and middle leaves before tasseling to gauge pustule density
Maintain balanced fertilization; avoid excess nitrogen without adequate potassium
prevention: Time planting to avoid flowering during extended cool, foggy morning periods
Practice field sanitation and weed host removal around field margins
treatment: Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L at the first sign of pustules on leaves below the ear
If disease spreads rapidly before silking, apply Propiconazole 25% EC @ 1.0 ml/L or Tebuconazole 25.9% EC @ 1.0 ml/L
safety_precautions: Follow 30-day PHI for grain corn and 14 days for sweet corn
Wear respiratory protection during spray preparation
source_references: ICAR-IIMR Maize Crop Protection Guidelines
TNAU Agritech Portal (Cereals - Maize Common Rust)

Corn___Northern_Leaf_Blight.overview: Northern Corn Leaf Blight (NCLB) is caused by Exserohilum turcicum. It creates large, cigar-shaped, grayish-green to tan lesions that can rapidly blight entire fields in wet, moderate temperatures.
symptoms: Large, elliptical or cigar-shaped tan lesions (3-15 cm long) with smooth margins
Lesions develop a dark, olivaceous velvety spore layer in damp weather
Extensive blighting of upper leaves reduces photosynthetic leaf area and ear filling
non_chemical_management: Till under corn residue post-harvest to reduce overwintering conidia
Rotate fields with non-host crops like legumes or oilseeds for 1-2 seasons
Ensure proper field drainage and avoid water stagnation
prevention: Choose NCLB-resistant corn hybrids with Ht resistance genes
Monitor weather forecasts during vegetative and silking stages
treatment: Apply Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Zineb 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L at early lesion detection
For rapid spread, apply Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Difenoconazole 11.4% SC @ 1.0 ml/L at threshold (3 lesions/leaf before tasseling)
safety_precautions: Adhere to label safety intervals; do not feed treated stover to livestock within 21 days of spraying
Use recommended spray pressure and nozzles for uniform canopy penetration
source_references: ICAR-IIMR Northern Corn Leaf Blight Management
TNAU Agritech Portal - Maize Diseases

Corn___healthy.overview: The corn foliage is robust, deep green, and free from leaf blights, rust pustules, and borer damage.
symptoms: Broad, erect green leaves without striping, necrosis, or spots
Strong stalk development with healthy ear formation
non_chemical_management: Apply split applications of nitrogen fertilizer to optimize plant uptake
Practice regular weed control during the critical first 30-45 days
Maintain optimal soil moisture during tasseling and silking stages
prevention: Follow balanced fertilization with zinc sulphate (25 kg/ha) at sowing
Scout weekly for fall armyworm and foliar blights
safety_precautions: No chemical fungicides or insecticides are needed for healthy maize foliage.
source_references: ICAR-IIMR Package of Practices for Maize Cultivation

Grape___Black_rot.overview: Black rot of grapes is caused by the fungus Guignardia bidwellii. It attacks all green parts of the vine, turning developing berries into hard, shriveled black mummies.
symptoms: Circular reddish-brown leaf spots with tiny black fruiting bodies (pycnidia) in rings
Black, elongated cankers on petioles and young canes
Berries turn pale, rot quickly, and shrivel into wrinkled, hard black mummies that remain attached
non_chemical_management: Prune out and destroy mummified berries and infected canes during dormant pruning
Trellis vines and train shoots to improve sunlight penetration and air movement
Disinfect pruning tools between vines
prevention: Avoid planting vines in shaded sites or near wild grape thickets
Ensure prompt canopy management and shoot tucking before bloom
treatment: Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 2.5 g/L from bud break to 4 weeks after bloom
Apply Myclobutanil 10% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 ml/L during high risk pre-bloom to post-bloom periods
safety_precautions: Maintain 21-day Pre-Harvest Interval for Difenoconazole
Do not spray copper during cool, wet conditions to avoid russeting on tender berries
source_references: ICAR-NRCG (National Research Centre for Grapes) Disease Advisory (https://nrcgrapes.icar.gov.in)
TNAU Agritech Portal (Horticulture - Grape Diseases)

Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).overview: Esca is a complex grapevine trunk disease caused by wood-decay fungi including Phaeoacremonium and Fomitiporia. It produces 'tiger-striped' leaves and speckled measles on berries.
symptoms: 'Tiger-stripe' chlorosis and interveinal necrosis on mature leaves
Small dark purple to brown speckles on berry skins ('measles')
Wood cross-sections reveal dark vascular streaking and spongy white heart rot in the trunk
non_chemical_management: Delay dormant pruning to late winter when wounds heal more quickly
Seal large pruning cuts immediately with an approved wound sealant or latex paint
Prune out symptomatic dead arms at least 10 cm into clean, white wood
Uproot and destroy severely declined, non-productive vines
prevention: Use certified disease-free rootstocks and scion wood from accredited nurseries
Minimize large pruning wounds on older cordons
treatment: No single curative systemic chemical exists for trunk wood decay inside mature vines
Apply pruning wound protectants containing Thiophanate-methyl paste or Trichoderma viride biocontrol agents
Maintain balanced vine irrigation and nutrition to alleviate physiological stress
safety_precautions: Do not spray excessive synthetic fungicides into canopy expecting to cure trunk decay
Always follow label precautions when applying wound paste
source_references: ICAR-NRCG Grapevine Trunk Disease Management Bulletin
University of California IPM - Grape Esca Complex

Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.overview: Isariopsis leaf spot is caused by Pseudocercospora cladosporioides (Isariopsis clavispora). It produces irregular brown leaf spots with distinct dark margins that cause premature defoliation in late summer.
symptoms: Irregular, angular reddish-brown to dark brown spots on upper leaf surfaces
Olive-brown to black velvety fungal growth on the underside of spots
Severely blighted leaves turn yellow, curl at the edges, and drop prematurely
non_chemical_management: Prune lower foliage and water shoots to elevate canopy and improve ventilation
Collect and compost or burn fallen infected leaves post-harvest
Maintain open canopy architecture with summer shoot positioning
prevention: Avoid dense vine training systems in humid tropical/subtropical regions
Scout canopies in mid-to-late season as foliage matures
treatment: Foliar spray of Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Bordeaux Mixture (1%)
Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Carbendazim 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L at first symptom notice
safety_precautions: Observe a 14-day Pre-Harvest Interval for synthetic fungicides
Wear eye protection and respirator when handling chemical powders
source_references: ICAR-NRCG Grape Disease Compendium
TNAU Agritech Portal (Horticulture - Grape Leaf Blight)

Grape___healthy.overview: The grape foliage is healthy, vibrant green, and free from powdery mildew, downy mildew, black rot, and trunk dieback.
symptoms: Uniform green leaf color with intact margins and clear veins
Healthy cane maturation and uniform berry cluster development
non_chemical_management: Maintain trellis wires and perform timely shoot thinning for ideal canopy exposure
Use drip irrigation under mulch to prevent soil splashing onto low foliage
Regulate crop load through cluster thinning to prevent vine exhaustion
prevention: Weekly scouting for downy mildew oil spots and powdery mildew flags
Annual dormant pruning to balance vegetative growth and fruitfulness
safety_precautions: No chemical fungicides or insecticides are needed for healthy grapevines.
source_references: ICAR-NRCG Best Management Practices for Viticulture

Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).overview: Huanglongbing (HLB) is caused by the phloem-restricted bacterium Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus, transmitted by the Asian citrus psyllid (Diaphorina citri). It causes blotchy leaf mottle, bitter misshapen fruit, and tree death.
symptoms: Asymmetrical, blotchy yellow mottle on mature leaves (unlike symmetrical zinc deficiency)
Yellowing of veins followed by vein corking
Small, lopsided, bitter fruits that stay green at the blossom end ('greening')
Dieback of twigs and eventual tree decline
non_chemical_management: Promptly uproot and destroy confirmed infected trees to eliminate regional bacterial reservoirs
Install yellow sticky traps (30-40 traps/ha) to monitor and catch Asian citrus psyllids
Release parasitoid wasps (Tamarixia radiata) for biological psyllid management
prevention: Plant only certified disease-free nursery saplings produced in insect-proof screenhouses
Quarantine movement of citrus budwood and seedlings from greening-endemic zones
treatment: There is no chemical cure for Liberibacter once a tree is infected; antibiotics do not eradicate the pathogen in field settings
Control the insect vector (psyllids) using Imidacloprid 17.8% SL @ 0.5 ml/L or Thiamethoxam 25% WG @ 0.3 g/L during new flushes
Foliar spray of micronutrients (Zinc, Iron, Manganese) to temporarily alleviate deficiency symptoms on neighboring uninfected trees
safety_precautions: Do NOT apply neonicotinoids during citrus blooming to avoid severe toxicity to honeybees
Consult local agriculture department or KVK immediately for quarantine confirmation
source_references: ICAR-CCRI (Central Citrus Research Institute) - HLB Management (https://ccri.icar.gov.in)
TNAU Agritech Portal (Horticulture - Citrus Greening)

Peach___Bacterial_spot.overview: Bacterial spot of peach is caused by Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni. It attacks leaves, twigs, and fruit, creating angular dark spots, 'shot-hole' perforations, and pitted fruit gumming.
symptoms: Small, water-soaked polygonal leaf spots that turn purplish-black
Centers of spots drop out, giving leaves a ragged 'shot-hole' appearance
Severe leaf yellowing and defoliation, especially at shoot tips
Pitted, sunken brown spots on peach skin with amber gum exudation
non_chemical_management: Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation that splashes bacteria across the canopy
Prune trees during dry weather to maintain good airflow and fast drying
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization that produces succulent, vulnerable shoots
prevention: Plant bacterial spot-tolerant peach varieties where available
Establish windbreaks in sandy soil sites to reduce blowing sand abrasions that enable bacterial entry
treatment: Apply Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 2.5 g/L during late dormant stage before bud swell
During growing season, apply low-rate Copper Hydroxide or Oxytetracycline / Streptocycline bactericide (where registered) at weekly intervals during wet weather
safety_precautions: Never apply high-dose copper after petal fall as peach foliage is highly sensitive to copper phytotoxicity
Observe all statutory harvest intervals
source_references: ICAR-CITH Stone Fruit Pathology Compendium
Clemson University Extension Peach Disease Guide

Peach___healthy.overview: The peach foliage is healthy, lanceolate, and vibrant green, without shot-holes, leaf curl, or bacterial lesions.
symptoms: Glossy, unblemished lanceolate leaves with intact margins
Healthy shoot growth without cankers or gummosis
non_chemical_management: Practice open-center pruning to maximize sunlight throughout the tree
Thin developing fruit to one fruit per 15-20 cm of branch for quality sizing
Mulch tree base with compost or organic matter to preserve soil moisture
prevention: Scout for peach leaf curl in early spring before bud break
Keep orchard borders weed-free to minimize insect vectors
safety_precautions: No chemical fungicides or insecticides are needed for healthy peach trees.
source_references: ICAR-CITH Good Agricultural Practices for Peach Orchards

Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.overview: Bacterial spot is caused by Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria. It thrives in hot, wet weather and produces water-soaked dark leaf lesions, defoliation, and rough raised fruit scabs.
symptoms: Small, water-soaked circular to irregular lesions on leaves turning dark brown with yellow halos
Severely spotted leaves turn yellow and drop prematurely, causing sunscald on exposed peppers
Raised, blister-like circular warts or scabs on bell pepper fruits
non_chemical_management: Use drip or furrow irrigation to keep bell pepper foliage completely dry
Destroy infected crop residues immediately after harvest; rotate away from solanaceous crops for 2 years
Work in fields only when plants are completely dry to prevent mechanical bacterial transmission
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed; soak seeds in hot water (50°C for 25 minutes) before sowing
Plant resistant bell pepper hybrids with multiple Bs race resistance genes
treatment: Foliar spray of Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 2.5 g/L mixed with Streptocycline @ 0.1 g/L at first notice
Alternatively, apply Kasugamycin 3% SL @ 1.5 ml/L or Copper Hydroxide 53.8% DF @ 2.0 g/L at 7-10 day intervals
safety_precautions: Observe a 7-day Pre-Harvest Interval before picking peppers
Wear protective chemical goggles, nitrile gloves, and face mask
source_references: ICAR-IIHR Pepper Pathology Bulletin
TNAU Agritech Portal (Vegetables - Bell Pepper Bacterial Spot)

Pepper,_bell___healthy.overview: The bell pepper foliage is rich green, firm, and completely free from bacterial spots, anthracnose, or viral mottling.
symptoms: Deep green leaves with smooth margins and no chlorotic spotting
Healthy branch branching with vigorous flower buds and fruit set
non_chemical_management: Maintain consistent drip irrigation to prevent blossom end rot and calcium deficiency
Stake plants or use trellis netting to support heavy fruit loads and prevent branch breakage
Apply reflective silver mulch to repel thrips and aphids while cooling root zone
prevention: Scout weekly for aphids, thrips, and mites on young terminal flushes
Ensure adequate soil calcium and avoid excessive ammonium-based nitrogen fertilizers
safety_precautions: No chemical pesticides or bactericides are needed for healthy bell pepper plants.
source_references: ICAR-IIHR Package of Practices for Capsicum Cultivation

Potato___Early_blight.overview: Potato early blight is caused by the fungus Alternaria solani. It targets older foliage, producing characteristic brown circular spots with concentric target-board rings.
symptoms: Dark brown to black angular spots on lower leaves with concentric rings ('target board')
Yellow halo around lesions leading to premature leaf drying and leaf drop
Sunken, dark, leathery dry rot lesions on potato tubers
non_chemical_management: Remove and destroy lower infected leaves during early crop development
Use drip irrigation to prevent prolonged leaf wetness from overhead sprinklers
Ensure proper vine hilling to prevent Alternaria spores from washing onto developing tubers
prevention: Rotate with non-solanaceous crops (cereals, legumes) for at least 2-3 years
Ensure balanced fertilization; avoid plant stress and nitrogen exhaustion during tuber bulking
treatment: Preventive spray: Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L
For established infections: Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 ml/L or Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 ml/L at 10-14 day intervals
safety_precautions: Maintain a 14-day Pre-Harvest Interval for Difenoconazole
Wear chemical gloves, goggles, and respirator during spraying
source_references: ICAR-CPRI (Central Potato Research Institute) - Disease Advisory (https://cpri.icar.gov.in)
TNAU Agritech Portal (Vegetables - Potato Early Blight)

Potato___Late_blight.overview: Potato late blight is caused by the oomycete Phytophthora infestans. It is an aggressive, destructive disease that thrives in cool, humid conditions, capable of blighting entire fields within days.
symptoms: Water-soaked, dark olive to brown irregular lesions on leaves and petioles
White, velvety fungal-like downy growth on the underside of leaves during high humidity
Rapid wilting, blackening, and foul-smelling collapse of canopy foliage
Tubers exhibit dry, granular, reddish-brown surface rot extending into the flesh
non_chemical_management: Eliminate potato cull piles and volunteer plants from previous seasons within 1 km
Hill up soil well (at least 10 cm over tubers) to prevent wash-down of sporangia
Cut and destroy vines (dehaulming) 10-14 days before harvest to allow tuber skins to harden
prevention: Plant certified disease-free seed tubers from accredited seed agencies
Choose late blight-tolerant varieties (e.g., Kufri Girdhari, Kufri Himalini)
Avoid overhead irrigation during cool, cloudy periods
treatment: Prophylactic protective spray: Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 3.0 g/L
Curative treatment at first sign: Metalaxyl 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP (Ridomil MZ) @ 2.5 g/L or Cymoxanil 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP @ 2.5 g/L
Dimethomorph 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Fenamidone 10% + Mancozeb 50% WG @ 2.5 g/L for severe pressure
safety_precautions: Observe a 14-day Pre-Harvest Interval for systemic fungicides
Do not exceed two consecutive applications of Metalaxyl to prevent fungicide resistance
Use full PPE: waterproof suit, chemical gloves, and organic vapor respirator
source_references: ICAR-CPRI Late Blight Management Bulletins (https://cpri.icar.gov.in)
TNAU Agritech Portal (Vegetables - Potato Late Blight)

Potato___healthy.overview: The potato canopy is lush, deep green, and free from early blight, late blight, and mosaic virus symptoms.
symptoms: Vigorous green foliage with erect stems and healthy leaflet margins
Clean root zone without tuber soft rots or brown rot lesions
non_chemical_management: Ensure proper hilling to protect developing tubers from sun-greening and tuber moth
Maintain uniform soil moisture during stolonization and tuber initiation
Avoid over-fertilizing with nitrogen which causes excessive haulm growth at the expense of tubers
prevention: Use certified seed tubers and practice crop rotation with cereals
Scout weekly for aphid vectors and early blight spots
safety_precautions: No chemical fungicides or insecticides are needed for healthy potato foliage.
source_references: ICAR-CPRI Good Agricultural Practices for Potato Production

Raspberry___healthy.overview: The raspberry canes exhibit healthy, clean green leaves without spur blight, cane blight, or anthracnose lesions.
symptoms: Vibrant green leaves with serrated margins and no purple or brown spotting
Sturdy primocanes and floricanes with healthy blossom and berry clusters
non_chemical_management: Trellis canes to improve air movement and facilitate rapid drying after rains
Prune out spent floricanes immediately after fruiting to improve sunlight penetration
Mulch with straw or wood chips to preserve root moisture and suppress weeds
prevention: Use drip irrigation under plastic or mulch to keep canes and foliage dry
Space rows adequately (2.5-3 meters) for optimum air movement
safety_precautions: No chemical fungicides or insecticides are needed for healthy raspberry plants.
source_references: University Horticultural Extension - Berry Health Guide

Soybean___healthy.overview: The soybean canopy is vigorous, uniformly green, and free from Asian soybean rust, frogeye leaf spot, and viral mosaics.
symptoms: Trifoliate leaves with vibrant green coloration and smooth margins
Strong nodulation on roots and healthy pod development
non_chemical_management: Inoculate seeds with Bradyrhizobium japonicum before planting for biological nitrogen fixation
Maintain optimal plant density (400,000 plants/ha) to prevent premature lodging
Keep fields weed-free during the critical first 30 days after emergence
prevention: Practice crop rotation with corn, wheat, or sorghum
Scout lower leaves regularly during the R1 to R5 reproductive stages
safety_precautions: No chemical interventions are needed for healthy soybean crops.
source_references: ICAR-IISR (Indian Institute of Soybean Research) Disease Management (https://iisrindore.icar.gov.in)

Squash___Powdery_mildew.overview: Squash powdery mildew is caused by Podosphaera xanthii and Erysiphe cichoracearum. It covers leaves in a white talcum-like powder, leading to yellowing, defoliation, and sunscalded squash.
symptoms: White circular powdery fungal spots on upper and lower leaf surfaces and petioles
Patches coalesce to cover entire leaves; leaves turn yellow, brown, and dry like paper
Premature defoliation leads to sunscald and reduced sugar content in fruit
non_chemical_management: Plant squash in full sunlight with wide spacing (1.5-2 meters between rows)
Remove and destroy heavily colonized older leaves at first sign of disease
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation; use drip lines at the base of vines
prevention: Choose powdery mildew-resistant cucurbit varieties
Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer that generates dense, susceptible vegetative growth
treatment: Apply Wettable Sulphur 80% WDG @ 2.5 g/L or Potassium Bicarbonate @ 3.0 g/L at first notice
For severe infections, apply Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 ml/L or Myclobutanil 10% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 ml/L
safety_precautions: Do NOT apply sulfur when ambient temperature exceeds 30°C to avoid severe phytotoxic burning of squash leaves
Observe a 7-day Pre-Harvest Interval before picking squash
source_references: ICAR-IIVR (Indian Institute of Vegetable Research) Cucurbit Protection Manual
TNAU Agritech Portal (Vegetables - Cucurbit Powdery Mildew)

Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.overview: Strawberry leaf scorch is caused by the fungus Diplocarpon earlianum. It produces numerous irregular purple blotches on leaves that enlarge and cause leaflets to dry and curl upward.
symptoms: Small, irregular purple to dark brown spots on the upper leaf surface without white centers
Spots coalesce, turning entire leaves purplish, brown, and scorched
Margins of leaflets curl upward; severe infections weaken crowns and reduce yield
non_chemical_management: Mow and rake beds after harvest (post-harvest renovation) and destroy infected foliage
Maintain narrow bed widths (30-40 cm) to encourage rapid drying of foliage
Use drip irrigation under straw or plastic mulch to keep leaves completely dry
prevention: Plant certified disease-free strawberry runners from accredited nurseries
Avoid establishing new plantings adjacent to older, diseased strawberry beds
treatment: Apply Captan 50% WP @ 2.0 g/L or Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L in early spring at new growth
Alternatively, apply Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 ml/L or Myclobutanil 10% WP @ 1.0 g/L if disease pressure is high
safety_precautions: Observe a 3-day Pre-Harvest Interval for Captan and 7 days for Azoxystrobin
Wear gloves and protective gear during application
source_references: ICAR-CITH Berry Fruit Pathology Bulletin
University of Florida Extension - Strawberry Leaf Scorch Management

Strawberry___healthy.overview: The strawberry foliage is healthy, tri-foliate, dark green, and free from leaf scorch, leaf spot, and gray mold.
symptoms: Deep green, glossy trifoliate leaves with clean, vibrant serrations
Sturdy crowns producing clean white flower blossoms and healthy berries
non_chemical_management: Mulch strawberry beds with clean straw to keep developing berries off bare soil
Ensure regular drip irrigation during flowering and fruit ripening
Remove dead or yellowing leaves during post-harvest bed renovation
prevention: Use raised beds covered with plastic mulch for superior drainage and weed control
Scout weekly for spider mites and gray mold on flower buds
safety_precautions: No chemical fungicides or insecticides are needed for healthy strawberry foliage.
source_references: ICAR-CITH Package of Practices for Strawberry Cultivation

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.overview: Bacterial spot is caused by Xanthomonas species (X. perforans, X. euvesicatoria). It causes water-soaked spots on leaves, stems, and fruits, resulting in severe defoliation during rainy, humid weather.
symptoms: Small (less than 3 mm), water-soaked, circular to angular dark brown spots on leaves
Lesions develop a yellow halo; severely infected leaves turn brown and drop
Black raised scabby spots on green and ripe tomato fruits
non_chemical_management: Avoid overhead irrigation; use drip irrigation to prevent water splash dissemination
Sterilize nursery trays, stakes, and pruning tools with 10% sodium hypochlorite
Immediately remove and burn or deeply bury heavily infected tomato plants
prevention: Use certified disease-free seeds; soak seeds in hot water (50°C for 25 minutes) before sowing
Rotate crops away from solanaceous species for at least 2-3 years
treatment: Spray Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 2.5 g/L mixed with Streptocycline @ 0.1 g/L
Alternatively, Copper Hydroxide 53.8% DF @ 2.0 g/L combined with Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L at 7-10 day intervals
safety_precautions: Observe a 7-day Pre-Harvest Interval before harvesting tomatoes
Wear chemical-resistant gloves, goggles, and face mask
source_references: ICAR-IIHR Tomato Disease Management Bulletins (https://iihr.res.in)
TNAU Agritech Portal (Horticulture - Tomato Bacterial Spot)

Tomato___Early_blight.overview: Early blight is a fungal disease caused by Alternaria solani. It primarily affects older foliage, creating dark brown circular spots with concentric target-board rings.
symptoms: Dark brown to black spots with concentric rings ('target board' pattern)
Yellowing of foliage surrounding the lesions
Lower leaves affected first, progressing upwards
Defoliation exposing fruit to sunscald
non_chemical_management: Prune and destroy infected lower leaves promptly
Apply organic straw mulch around plant base to prevent soil splash
Ensure proper plant spacing (60 x 45 cm) for canopy aeration
Use drip or furrow irrigation to keep foliage dry
prevention: Rotate crops away from solanaceous plants (potato, chilli, brinjal) for 2-3 years
Use certified disease-free seeds and vigorous seedlings
Clean and disinfect staking poles and pruning tools
treatment: Foliar spray of Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L at the first appearance of symptoms
Alternatively, Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L at 10-14 day intervals
For severe infections, Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 ml/L or Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 ml/L
safety_precautions: Wear protective gloves, eye protection, and mask during chemical application
Observe a mandatory Pre-Harvest Interval (PHI) of 7-10 days before harvesting fruit
Avoid spraying during windy conditions or midday peak heat
source_references: ICAR-IIHR Tomato Disease Guide (https://iihr.res.in)
TNAU Agritech Portal (Horticulture - Tomato Diseases)

Tomato___Late_blight.overview: Late blight is a fast-spreading oomycete disease caused by Phytophthora infestans. It develops rapidly in cool, wet weather and can destroy foliage and fruits within days.
symptoms: Water-soaked, dark olive to brown irregular lesions on leaves and stems
White fungal downy growth on the underside of leaves in high humidity
Rapid wilting and collapse of leaves appearing frost-damaged
Greasy, dark brown firm rot on green and ripe tomato fruits
non_chemical_management: Immediately prune and bury heavily infected shoots outside the field
Stake tomato vines and avoid dense canopy shading
Eliminate volunteer tomato plants and potato cull piles nearby
prevention: Plant resistant or tolerant tomato varieties where available
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation
Ensure rapid field drainage during heavy rains
treatment: Preventive spray: Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 3.0 g/L
Curative spray upon first lesions: Metalaxyl 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP @ 2.5 g/L
Alternatively, Dimethomorph 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Cymoxanil 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP @ 2.5 g/L
safety_precautions: Do not spray Metalaxyl more than twice per season to prevent resistant pathogen strains
Observe Pre-Harvest Interval of 7-14 days depending on product label
Wear chemical-resistant gloves, boots, and face protection
source_references: ICAR-IIHR Late Blight Management Bulletins
TNAU Agritech Portal - Tomato Late Blight

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.overview: Leaf mold is caused by Passalora fulva (formerly Cladosporium fulvum). It thrives in high humidity (above 85%), especially in protected polyhouses and greenhouses.
symptoms: Pale greenish-yellow chlorotic spots on upper leaf surfaces
Olive-green to brown velvety fungal mold on the lower leaf surface corresponding to spots
Infected leaves wither, roll, turn brown, and drop prematurely
non_chemical_management: Maximize greenhouse or polyhouse ventilation with exhaust fans and louvers
Maintain relative humidity below 85% through proper spacing and drip watering
Prune lower foliage and suckers to encourage airflow through the canopy
prevention: Choose leaf mold-resistant tomato varieties with Cf resistance genes
Disinfect greenhouse frames and polyethylene film between crop cycles
treatment: Apply Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L
For severe greenhouse outbreaks, spray Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 ml/L or Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 ml/L
safety_precautions: Ensure full greenhouse ventilation before re-entering after chemical spraying
Follow 7-day Pre-Harvest Interval for edible tomatoes
source_references: ICAR-IIHR Protected Vegetable Cultivation Bulletins
TNAU Agritech Portal (Tomato Leaf Mold)

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.overview: Septoria leaf spot is caused by Septoria lycopersici. It creates numerous small, circular spots with dark brown margins and gray centers containing tiny black pycnidia.
symptoms: Numerous small (1.5-3 mm) circular spots with dark brown borders and grayish-white centers
Tiny black specks (pycnidia) clearly visible in the center of mature lesions
Leaves turn yellow, wither, and drop, starting from the lowest branches upward
non_chemical_management: Remove and destroy lower infected leaves as soon as first spots appear
Apply thick straw or plastic mulch to prevent rain/irrigation water splash from soil
Stake and cage plants to keep foliage off the ground
prevention: Rotate tomato fields for 2-3 years away from solanaceous crops
Control solanaceous weeds (e.g., black nightshade, Solanum nigrum) around field borders
treatment: Foliar spray of Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L or Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L
Apply Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 2.5 g/L at 7-10 day intervals during wet weather
safety_precautions: Follow Pre-Harvest Interval of 7 days before picking tomatoes
Avoid spraying in high wind to avoid drift to non-target areas
source_references: ICAR-IIHR Tomato Protection Bulletins
TNAU Agritech Portal - Tomato Septoria Spot

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.overview: Two-spotted spider mites (Tetranychus urticae) are microscopic sap-sucking arachnids. They feed on plant cell contents, causing fine yellow stippling, bronzing, and silken webbing.
symptoms: Fine yellow or white stippling on the upper leaf surface
Leaves turn bronze, dry, brittle, and drop under heavy infestation
Fine, delicate silken webbing covering the undersides of leaves and growing tips
Tiny moving yellow-red mites visible under 10x magnification
non_chemical_management: Spray undersides of leaves with strong water jets to knock down mite populations and destroy webs
Release predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis or Neoseiulus californicus) for biological control
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization and prevent dusty, dry conditions around field borders
prevention: Apply overhead misting or maintain adequate field humidity during hot, dry spells
Eliminate weed hosts (pigweed, amaranthus) around field borders
treatment: Foliar spray of Neem oil (Azadirachtin 10,000 ppm) @ 3.0 ml/L or Insecticidal Soap @ 5.0 ml/L
For severe outbreaks, apply Spiromesifen 22.9% SC @ 1.0 ml/L or Propargite 57% EC @ 2.0 ml/L or Abamectin 1.9% EC @ 0.5 ml/L
safety_precautions: Do NOT use broad-spectrum synthetic pyrethroids which kill beneficial predatory mites and flare spider mite outbreaks
Observe a 7-day Pre-Harvest Interval for Spiromesifen
source_references: ICAR-NBAIR (National Bureau of Agricultural Insect Resources) - Mite Advisory
TNAU Agritech Portal (Horticulture - Tomato Spider Mites)

Tomato___Target_Spot.overview: Target spot is caused by the fungus Corynespora cassiicola. It creates circular brown lesions with distinct concentric rings on leaves, stems, and fruits in warm, humid regions.
symptoms: Small, pinpoint brown spots expanding into circular lesions (up to 10 mm) with light brown centers
Lesions show faint concentric rings surrounded by yellow halos
Dark, sunken, circular lesions with velvety centers on green and ripe tomato fruits
non_chemical_management: Prune suckers and lower leaves to improve canopy aeration and expedite leaf drying
Avoid overhead irrigation; install drip systems beneath mulch
Collect and destroy crop debris immediately after final harvest
prevention: Maintain wide plant spacing (60 x 60 cm) to prevent dense canopy humidity
Rotate crops away from solanaceous plants and cucurbits for 2 seasons
treatment: Foliar spray of Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L or Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L
For severe pressure: Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 ml/L or Boscalid + Pyraclostrobin @ 1.0 g/L
safety_precautions: Follow product-specific Pre-Harvest Intervals (7 days for Chlorothalonil)
Wear protective chemical gear during application
source_references: ICAR-IIHR Tomato Disease Bulletins
University of Florida Extension - Tomato Target Spot Management

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.overview: Tomato Mosaic Virus (ToMV) is a mechanically transmitted Tobamovirus. It spreads easily via workers' hands, tools, clothes, and seeds, causing leaf mottling, distortion, and stunted growth.
symptoms: Mottled light and dark green mosaic patterns on leaves
Leaf distortion, blistering, puckering, and 'shoestring' or fern-like thinning of leaflets
Stunted plant growth and uneven ripening with internal brown fruit necrosis
non_chemical_management: Immediately rogue (uproot) and destroy infected plants; do NOT compost them
Workers must wash hands and dip tools in 10% non-fat dry milk solution or 10% trisodium phosphate (TSP) before touching plants
Prohibit tobacco use near greenhouse or field tomato plants (tobacco can carry virus particles)
prevention: Plant ToMV-resistant tomato varieties (designated with 'Tm-2' or 'ToMV')
Use certified virus-free seed; heat-treat seeds at 70°C for 2-4 days where feasible
Control solanaceous weeds around field borders
treatment: There are NO chemical pesticides or curative treatments that cure viral plant infections
Do NOT spray synthetic fungicides or antibiotics; they are completely ineffective against viruses
Focus entirely on sanitation, tool disinfection, and prompt rogueing of symptomatic plants
safety_precautions: Do NOT apply synthetic agrochemicals based on viral diagnoses.
Sanitize hands and tools frequently to prevent mechanical transmission.
source_references: ICAR-IIHR Plant Virology Bulletins
TNAU Agritech Portal (Horticulture - Tomato Mosaic Virus)

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.overview: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV) is a devastating begomovirus transmitted by the sweetpotato whitefly (Bemisia tabaci). It causes severe stunting, erect yellow cupped leaves, and floral abortion.
symptoms: Upward curling and cupping of leaflets with prominent yellowing (chlorosis) of margins
Severe reduction in leaf size giving a bushy, stunted appearance
Flower drop (abscission) leading to near-total failure of fruit set
non_chemical_management: Rogue and bury infected plants immediately inside sealed plastic bags to prevent whiteflies from escaping
Install yellow sticky traps (40-50 traps/ha) across the field to monitor and mass-trap whiteflies
Grow seedlings under 40-50 mesh insect-proof net tunnels for the first 30 days
prevention: Plant TYLCV-resistant tomato hybrids (e.g., US 440, NS 501, Abhinav)
Use reflective silver mulches to repel incoming whiteflies during early vegetative growth
Maintain a host-free fallow period between solanaceous crop cycles
treatment: Chemical treatments cannot cure the virus inside the plant; management targets the whitefly vector
Foliar spray of Neem oil (Azadirachtin 10,000 ppm) @ 3.0 ml/L to deter whitefly feeding
To control high whitefly populations: Imidacloprid 17.8% SL @ 0.5 ml/L or Thiamethoxam 25% WG @ 0.3 g/L or Spiromesifen 22.9% SC @ 1.0 ml/L
safety_precautions: Do not apply neonicotinoid sprays during open bloom to protect honeybees and pollinators
Adhere strictly to Pre-Harvest Interval of 7 days before fruit harvesting
source_references: ICAR-IIHR Tomato Begomovirus Advisory (https://iihr.res.in)
TNAU Agritech Portal (Horticulture - Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl)

Tomato___healthy.overview: The tomato foliage is healthy, deep green, robust, and completely free from foliar blights, viral mottling, and spider mite stippling.
symptoms: Vibrant, dark green compound leaves with erect petioles
Sturdy main stems, active flowering clusters, and uniform green fruit set
non_chemical_management: Stake or cage tomato plants and remove bottom suckers up to the first flower cluster
Apply drip irrigation under organic straw mulch to keep root zone evenly moist
Maintain balanced nutrition with calcium nitrate to prevent blossom end rot
prevention: Weekly field scouting to detect early signs of whiteflies, leafminers, or blight spots
Sanitize pruning shears between plants
safety_precautions: No chemical fungicides or insecticides are needed for healthy tomato plants.
source_references: ICAR-IIHR Good Agricultural Practices for Tomato Cultivation
